screens.title: Developing Basic Smart Contracts
screens.subtitle: A friendly introduction to Solidity, Remix IDE, and building your first contracts

narration.text: In this chapter you will begin writing real smart contracts using Solidity and the Remix IDE. Solidity is a statically typed, contract-oriented language tailored for Ethereum-style blockchains. We'll explain why a pragma directive matters, how contracts hold state with variables, and how functions read and update that state. You will also learn to use Remix as a zero-setup browser environment to compile, deploy, and interact with contracts on a simulated chain. Practically, you'll see a working example that stores and returns a number, and then you'll complete a hands-on counter exercise. Throughout, pay attention to visibility keywords and the difference between functions that change state and functions that only read it. That difference determines whether an interaction consumes gas. By the end of this chapter you will be able to write a minimal contract, compile it, deploy it in Remix, and observe state changes. Think about why the blockchain makes state changes permanent, and how that permanence changes how you design functions and guard access.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: You will move from theory to practice by writing a Solidity contract, learning the compiler and Remix workflow, and understanding how state and visibility affect deployment and gas.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain and why they matter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will accomplish four practical skills. First, you will understand the purpose and basic syntax of Solidity: what a pragma is, what a contract looks like, and why state variables and functions are defined the way they are. That foundation helps you read and write simple contracts safely. Second, you will learn to use the Remix IDE so you can compile, deploy, and debug without installing tooling. This matters because a reproducible browser workflow speeds iteration and lowers setup friction for beginners. Third, you will construct a simple Solidity contract with pragmas, state variables, and functions, then deploy it and observe state changes in the JavaScript VM. You will see the difference between view functions and state-modifying transactions. Fourth, you will work through a hands-on counter exercise that enforces concepts like function visibility and require checks. This final skill builds confidence and prepares you for more complex DApp development. Each objective ties to practice: compile code, deploy to a simulated chain, and interact to see persistent state.

keyIdea.title: Practical outcomes

screens.title: What you will practice
screens.subtitle: Hands-on activities and checks for understanding

narration.text: This chapter pairs explanation with hands-on practice so you can confirm understanding. You will compile and deploy a minimal storage contract and then complete a counter exercise with TODOs to enforce concept mastery. The practice targets concrete skills: declaring a pragma and selecting a compatible compiler, using correct data types for state variables such as uint256 and address, and distinguishing functions that are view-only from ones that require transactions. The exercises also require you to guard state changes using runtime checks, for example preventing a counter from decrementing below zero using a require statement. Each exercise is designed so that a failed test reveals a specific misconception: mixing up visibility levels, forgetting to mark a reader function as view, or misusing string types for short fixed-size data. Working through these activities in Remix's JavaScript VM helps you see transaction receipts and how gas is consumed, all without needing real tokens. By practicing, you'll build habits that prevent common beginner errors as you scale to larger contracts.

screens.title: What is Solidity?
screens.subtitle: A contract-oriented, statically typed language for Ethereum

narration.text: Solidity is a high-level programming language purpose-built for writing smart contracts that run on Ethereum and compatible virtual machines. When we say contract-oriented we mean the language revolves around a contract unit, similar to a class that encapsulates state variables and functions. Statically typed means that variable types are declared and checked at compile time, which helps catch errors earlier but also requires explicit choices about storage and sizes. Solidity looks syntactically similar to JavaScript, which lowers the learning curve, but includes blockchain-specific types like address and modifiers for function behavior such as view or payable. Code you write in Solidity is compiled down to EVM bytecode; that bytecode is what nodes execute. A practical example of why this matters: choosing uint256 for a counter ensures predictable arithmetic range and storage layout. Misconceptions to avoid: Solidity is not a scripting language you run locally — it compiles to bytecode executed on the EVM, and state changes require transactions and gas. Reflect: as you write your first contract, consider how static typing and contract structure change how you design functions and guard state changes.

keyIdea.title: Core claim
keyIdea.text: Solidity is a statically typed, contract-oriented language whose types and modifiers express on-chain behavior and gas implications.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is Solidity?
Definition

Contract-oriented and statically typed

Solidity uses contracts to group state and behavior. Types like uint256, address, and bool are explicit, so the compiler can check them before deployment.

Analogy: contract as a wooden chest
State variables are drawers; functions are keys that open or change those drawers under rules you write.
Example
Choosing uint256 for counters avoids unexpected wrap behavior on modern compilers and matches typical storage expectations.
Misconception
Do not assume JavaScript semantics carry over. Solidity's types and gas model change how you structure logic.
Quick reference
Type
uint256
Common for counters and numeric state.
Type
address
Stores 20-byte account or contract identifiers.
Modifier
view
Function that reads state without changing it; no gas when called locally.
Keyword
public
Creates an external getter for state variables and allows external calls to functions.
Key Takeaway

Solidity's types and modifiers encode how code behaves on-chain; design choices affect gas, safety, and accessibility.

screens.title: Remix IDE: compile, deploy, interact
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step workflow to test contracts in a JavaScript VM

narration.text: Remix provides an integrated workflow that lets you write Solidity, compile it, deploy to a local simulated chain, and call contract functions without installing any tools. Start by creating a new file in the file explorer and adding a pragma to establish the intended compiler range. Next, open the Solidity Compiler panel and select a compiler compatible with your pragma; compiling reports syntax and type errors that you fix before deployment. After successful compilation, switch to the Deploy & Run panel. Choose the JavaScript VM environment to run a browser-hosted node where transactions simulate gas consumption and produce receipts. Select the compiled contract factory, click deploy, and watch the deployed instance appear in the panel. Expand the deployed contract to see automatically generated getters for public state variables and buttons for each function. For functions that change state you'll enter input values and send a transaction, which consumes gas in the simulated environment and shows a transaction log. For view functions, call them to read state without gas. A common misconception is thinking that calling any function will cost gas — only transactions that modify state require gas. Practice this process until you can consistently compile, deploy, and observe how state changes appear in logs and getters.

screens.title: Pragma directive and compiler versions
screens.subtitle: Why lock a compiler version and how to express it

narration.text: A pragma directive at the top of a Solidity file declares which compiler versions are compatible with the code you write. Writing that directive is important because language features and safety checks evolve between compiler releases. The typical form uses a caret and a version number, which means the code is compatible with that version and newer minor revisions but not with the next major release. For example, a pragma indicating version zero point eight point zero tells the compiler to accept versions at least zero point eight point zero but less than zero point nine point zero. This prevents accidental compilation with a vastly different compiler that might change behavior. A common beginner mistake is omitting the pragma or selecting a mismatched compiler in the IDE, which leads to confusing errors or subtle behavioral changes. When you open the compiler panel in Remix, confirm that the selected compiler falls within your pragma range before compiling. If you need to use a newer language feature, update the pragma and choose a matching compiler version. Always treat the pragma as a compatibility contract between your source and the compiler implementation.

keyIdea.title: Pragma purpose
keyIdea.text: The pragma protects you from compiling with an incompatible compiler version and helps ensure consistent behavior across toolchains.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Pragma Directive
Pragma

A single line that defines compatibility with compiler versions. Treat it as a contract between your code and the compiler implementation.

Example directive
// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;
The caret indicates compatibility with 0.8.x releases but not 0.9.x.
Why it matters
Compiler behavior affects safety checks, optimizations, and available language features.
Common mistake
Using a compiler outside the pragma range leads to errors or unexpected differences in how operations behave.
Checklist
  • Include a pragma in every file.
  • Match the compiler version in Remix to the pragma range.
  • Update pragma intentionally when using new features.
Key Takeaway

Pragma keeps your source and compiler in agreement, reducing surprises during compilation and deployment.

screens.title: Contract structure: state variables and functions
screens.subtitle: How contracts hold and expose data, and how functions change or read it

narration.text: A Solidity contract groups two main elements: state variables and functions. State variables represent persistent data stored on-chain; when a transaction updates them, the new value is written into contract storage and persists across subsequent calls. Functions are executable units that either read state or modify it. We distinguish view functions, which promise not to modify state, from state-changing functions that require transactions and gas. Visibility keywords such as public, private, internal, and external control who can call a function or access a variable. A public state variable automatically creates a getter function, which is why declaring a variable public is a common shortcut for read access. Think about a token balance mapping: mapping from addresses to uint256 is stored and read often, but only specific functions should be allowed to change those balances. Misunderstandings often come from treating state reads and writes the same: reads can be done locally without gas when marked view, while writes always create a transaction. When designing contracts, plan which functions modify state and which only return values, and enforce access using visibility and require checks.

keyIdea.title: Design principle
keyIdea.text: Separate read-only behaviors from state-changing actions and use visibility and checks to protect state transitions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Contract Structure
Architecture

State variables and functions

State variables store persistent data on-chain. Functions read or change that data, and visibility determines accessibility.

State example
uint256 public storedData; creates a storage slot and an automatic getter.
Function roles
Functions marked view return values without changing state; other functions send transactions to modify state and consume gas.
Misconception
A public getter does not mean the underlying storage is changeable by anyone; that depends on which functions you expose for writes.
Example card
Simple storage pattern
Declare a uint256 state variable, add a set function to update it, and a view get function to read it. Writes require a transaction, reads marked view do not.
Key Takeaway

Plan state layout and function visibility before writing business logic to reduce security and gas issues.

screens.title: SimpleStorage example explained
screens.subtitle: A line-by-line walkthrough of a minimal contract

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal contract that stores and returns a number. The file begins with a license identifier comment and the pragma that pins the compiler range. Next the contract keyword names the contract body where you declare a state variable of type uint256 that is marked public. Marking it public is convenient because the compiler generates a getter function for you, enabling external read access without extra code. The set function takes a uint256 argument and assigns it to the state variable; because it modifies state it requires a transaction when invoked and consumes gas. The get function is marked view and returns the current stored value; calling it does not change state and therefore can be executed as a free read in the Remix interface. A useful practical note: when you call set in Remix you'll see a transaction receipt in the console and the storedData getter will reflect the updated value only after the transaction completes. A common confusion is thinking view functions consume gas — they do not when invoked locally for reading. As you read the code, consider permissions and whether functions should be public or restricted in real contracts.

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough summary
keyIdea.text: Public state variables create getters; set modifies storage and requires gas; view functions read state without gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › SimpleStorage Walkthrough
Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
    // State variable to store a number
    uint256 public storedData; // 'public' creates an automatic getter function

    // Function to set the value of storedData
    function set(uint256 x) public {
        storedData = x;
    }

    // Function to retrieve the value of storedData
    function get() public view returns (uint256) {
        return storedData;
    }
}
Annotations
  • SPDX & pragma: license and compiler range set expectations for tools.
  • storedData: a public uint256 state variable with an automatic getter.
  • set(x): updates state and therefore creates a transaction; watch gas usage in Remix.
  • get(): declared view and returns state without modifying the blockchain.
Key Takeaway

A minimal contract demonstrates storage, automatic getters, state updates via transactions, and view-only reads for free inspection.

screens.title: Solidity data types overview
screens.subtitle: Common types: uint, address, bool, string, bytes, mapping, struct, enum

narration.text: Solidity includes several fundamental data types you will use frequently. Unsigned integers like uint and uint256 are standard for counts and balances. Addresses represent 20-byte identifiers for accounts or contracts and are essential when storing ownership or transferring value. Booleans represent true/false flags. Strings hold text but can be gas-intensive; for short fixed-length content prefer bytes types like bytes32. Mapping acts as a key-value store mapping from primitive types such as address to another type, useful for balances or permissions. Structs let you group multiple fields into a single custom type, and enums define a set of named constants when you need a restricted set of states. Each type has trade-offs: strings are flexible but costly, fixed-size bytes are cheaper to store, and mappings are efficient but do not allow iteration over keys. When designing state layout, pick types that balance expressiveness with gas and storage costs. A common misconception is to use strings everywhere; in most contract logic, numeric and fixed-size types are more appropriate. Consider how you will read and write data and choose types accordingly. Solidity data types overview means choose types for both correctness and efficiency: prefer fixed-size and numeric types for frequent on-chain operations and guard expensive string usage.. In practical terms, common types: uint, address, bool, string, bytes, mapping, struct, enum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Type selection matters
keyIdea.text: Choose types for both correctness and efficiency: prefer fixed-size and numeric types for frequent on-chain operations and guard expensive string usage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Data Types
Common types
uint / uint256
Unsigned integers for counters and balances.
address
20-byte account or contract identifier used for ownership and transfers.
bool
True/false flags for simple logic.
string / bytes
Use bytes for short, fixed-length data; strings are flexible but costly.
mapping
Key-value storage like address → uint256 for balances; efficient but not iterable.
struct / enum
Custom grouped types and restricted named states.
Practical guidance
  • Choose uint256 for counters unless storage/packing reasons require smaller types.
  • Avoid using strings for frequently-written state.
  • Use mappings for lookups and structs for grouped data.
Key Takeaway

Type choices influence gas and usability; favor efficient fixed-size types for on-chain operations.

screens.title: Deploying and interacting with SimpleStorage
screens.subtitle: What you will observe when you deploy and call functions in Remix

narration.text: When you deploy the SimpleStorage contract in Remix's JavaScript VM you will see a fresh instance appear under Deployed Contracts. Initially the public storedData getter usually returns zero because the state variable is uninitialized. Calling the set function with a value sends a transaction to the simulated chain; you will be prompted to confirm a transaction in the UI, and a receipt will appear in the console showing gas used and a transaction hash. After the transaction is mined by the local VM, calling storedData or get will return the updated value. In the Remix UI the public state variable appears as both a labeled getter button and the get function is available if provided. A key learning point is observing transaction lifecycles: you send a state-changing call, it consumes gas and generates a receipt, then state is updated on-chain. Calling view functions returns immediately without gas and shows the current storage value. Try calling set with a value like forty-two, inspect the console for a transaction log, and then call get to confirm the change. This concrete experiment links code to on-chain behavior and reinforces the difference between reads and writes.

keyIdea.title: Runtime insight
keyIdea.text: State changes occur only after a transaction completes; view calls return state instantly without consuming gas in the simulated environment.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Deploy & Interact
Observation steps
  1. Deploy contract to JavaScript VM and expand the instance.
  2. Call the public getter to note the initial value.
  3. Use set with an input like 42 and send the transaction.
  4. Inspect the transaction receipt and then call get again to confirm the new state.
What the console shows
Gas used, transaction hash, and logs. The receipt verifies the state change after mining on the simulated chain.
Try this
Deploy SimpleStorage, call set with 42, inspect the transaction details, then call get to confirm the value persists. Note the difference in behavior between set and get.
Key Takeaway

Transactions change state and produce receipts; view reads return state immediately without gas in the simulated environment.

screens.title: Common mistakes and visibility pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Visibility specifiers, overflow, and accidental exposure

narration.text: Beginners commonly make a few recurring mistakes that can lead to bugs or vulnerabilities. First, visibility specifiers control who can call functions or access variables. Declaring functions or variables public exposes them to external calls and automatic getters, which is convenient for reads but risky for sensitive state. Consider who should be allowed to change state and mark functions appropriately or use access checks. Second, integer overflow and underflow historically allowed arithmetic to wrap around; since Solidity zero point eight point zero, arithmetic checks are automatic, but older code must be audited for vulnerabilities. Third, confusion about view versus state-changing functions can cause unexpected gas costs; calling a modifying function will always create a transaction and consume gas. Fourth, using strings for frequently updated storage can be unexpectedly expensive. Lastly, mapping types are not iterable; developers sometimes try to loop keys and discover it’s not supported. A useful habit is to think explicitly about who can call each function, add require checks to enforce preconditions, and prefer explicit returns for read-only functions. When in doubt, mark a function view if it only reads state, and avoid making mutating functions public unless necessary and protected.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Control visibility, prefer checks like require for preconditions, and be aware of older overflow issues and the cost of string storage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Common Mistakes
Visibility & errors
Visibility confusion
Public creates getters; avoid making mutating functions public without access controls.
Overflow/underflow
Modern compilers check arithmetic, but audit older contracts that may wrap values.
Expensive strings
Use bytes for short, fixed-length data to save gas.
Preventative steps
  • Add require checks for preconditions.
  • Restrict mutating functions via visibility and modifiers.
  • Test edge cases in Remix before deploying publicly.
Common pitfall

Making everything public for convenience can unintentionally expose state-changing capabilities to anyone.

screens.title: Counter exercise: starter code and TODOs
screens.subtitle: Complete the TODOs in Counter.sol and test edge cases in Remix

narration.text: This hands-on task asks you to create a Counter contract with TODO markers. The starter code declares a contract and leaves four TODOs: declare a public uint256 count, create an increment function that increases count, create a decrement function that decreases count with a require guard so count cannot go negative, and add a getCount view function that returns the current value. The exercise is designed to reinforce state variable declaration, writing state-changing functions, and using require to prevent invalid state transitions. After filling in the TODOs, compile with a matching compiler, deploy to the JavaScript VM, and test the flow: call getCount to confirm the initial zero value, call increment several times and verify the count increases, then call decrement and confirm the require prevents decrementing below zero. If you call decrement at zero you should see an error message matching the require statement. This immediate feedback in Remix helps you connect code to runtime behavior and reinforces the importance of runtime checks when mutating stored state. Counter exercise: starter code and TODOs means implement safe increment and decrement operations and verify that runtime checks prevent invalid state transitions in remix.. In practical terms, complete the todos in counter.sol and test edge cases in remix. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Exercise goal
keyIdea.text: Implement safe increment and decrement operations and verify that runtime checks prevent invalid state transitions in Remix.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Counter Exercise
Starter code (place in Counter.sol)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    // TODO 1: Declare a public state variable named 'count' of type uint256.
    // It should be initialized to 0 by default.

    // TODO 2: Create a public function named 'increment' that increases 'count' by 1.
    // This function will change the state of the blockchain.

    // TODO 3: Create a public view function named 'decrement' that decreases 'count' by 1.
    // Add a 'require' statement to ensure 'count' does not go below 0.
    // This function will also change the state of the blockchain.

    // TODO 4: Create a public view function named 'getCount' that returns the current value of 'count'.
    // This function does not change the state.
}
Instructions
Fill each TODO, compile with a matching compiler, deploy to JavaScript VM, then test increment and decrement, and confirm require prevents negative counts.
Check your understanding

After implementation, what happens when you call decrement at zero? Why is require important here?

screens.title: Counter solution and explanations
screens.subtitle: A correct implementation with rationale for each choice

narration.text: Here is a straightforward solution that fulfills the Counter exercise. First, declare a public uint256 count which initializes to zero automatically. The increment function increases count by one and modifies state; it should be public so external callers can trigger it during testing. The decrement function must prevent underflow: include a require statement that ensures count is greater than zero before decrementing. The getCount function is declared view and returns the current count; it does not consume gas when read locally. This solution emphasizes clear intent and runtime safety: using require enforces preconditions at the moment of state change and gives a meaningful error message when the precondition fails. When you deploy and test in Remix, incrementing several times then decrementing shows state changes reflected in getCount. If you attempt to decrement at zero, Remix will surface the require error. Remember that marking state variables public is convenient for testing, but in production you may want finer-grained access control. This exercise reinforces how to declare state, write state-changing logic with guards, and provide efficient read-only access. Counter solution and explanations means use require to enforce runtime rules, separate view reads from state-changing writes, and choose visibility deliberately for testing versus production.. In practical terms, a correct implementation with rationale for each choice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Solution insight
keyIdea.text: Use require to enforce runtime rules, separate view reads from state-changing writes, and choose visibility deliberately for testing versus production.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Counter Solution
Expected solution
// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    // TODO 1: Declare a public state variable named 'count' of type uint256.
    uint256 public count;

    // TODO 2: Create a public function named 'increment' that increases 'count' by 1.
    function increment() public {
        count++;
    }

    // TODO 3: Create a public view function named 'decrement' that decreases 'count' by 1.
    // Add a 'require' statement to ensure 'count' does not go below 0.
    function decrement() public {
        require(count > 0, "Count cannot be negative");
        count--;
    }

    // TODO 4: Create a public view function named 'getCount' that returns the current value of 'count'.
    function getCount() public view returns (uint256) {
        return count;
    }
}
Rationale
  • uint256 is the conventional unsigned integer for counters.
  • increment modifies state, so it is a transaction and not view.
  • decrement uses require to prevent invalid negative state transitions.
  • getCount is view and returns state without gas when called locally.
Key Takeaway

Clear guards and explicit view declarations make contracts safer and easier to test in Remix before deploying widely.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Let's review three essential ideas. First, Solidity is a statically typed, contract-oriented language whose types and modifiers express on-chain behavior; choose types like uint256 and address deliberately. Second, Remix IDE provides a no-setup environment to write, compile, deploy to a JavaScript VM, and observe transactions and state changes. This workflow is invaluable for quick iteration and debugging. Third, distinguish view functions from state-changing functions: view reads do not alter state and do not consume gas when called locally, while state-changing functions require transactions and gas and must include runtime guards like require to prevent invalid transitions. These three principle reminders—type choices, the Remix test loop, and the read-versus-write distinction—will guide your first contracts and help you avoid common beginner mistakes such as wrong compiler versions, public exposure of mutating functions, or missing runtime checks. Keep these in mind as you advance to more complex contract patterns.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Types, Remix workflow, and the distinction between reads and writes form the foundation for safe, testable contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
Solidity Types
Pick uint, address, bytes, and structs with gas and semantics in mind.
Remix IDE
Compile, deploy to the JavaScript VM, and inspect transaction receipts.

Summary
